title: Talking therapy (CBT) for anxiety
description: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is the most studied talking therapy for anxiety disorders. It helps people test anxious predictions and face what they fear step by step. The episode shows three views of the change: pooled across anxiety disorders, while facing a social threat, and while deliberately rethinking a negative thought. In the first part, brightness shows how the brain differed from people without anxiety before treatment. After that, brightness shows the change since before treatment: warmer means more than before, violet means less than before.
caveat: The pooled findings come from an analysis of 22 studies of CBT for depression and anxiety disorders; the anxiety studies cover several different disorders. The two other parts come from single studies of social anxiety disorder, one of 14 people with no untreated comparison group (so the changes cannot be credited to CBT alone) and one randomised trial of 75 people of whom about 60 had usable scans, using different tasks, which is why the medial prefrontal cortex goes down in one and up in the other. The pooled analysis names the superior frontal gyrus, which is not drawn as its own area. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before treatment, people with social anxiety showed more activity than people without it in the right medial prefrontal cortex and right insula when looking at angry faces.

phases.name: A course of CBT
phases.caption: Twelve to sixteen weekly sessions. People were not scanned during this time.

citations.authors: Klumpp H, Fitzgerald DA, Phan KL
citations.title: Neural predictors and mechanisms of cognitive behavioral therapy on threat processing in social anxiety disorder.
citations.quote: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was conducted during responses to social signals of threat (fearful/angry faces) against positive signals (happy faces) in 14 patients with SAD before and after 12 weeks of CBT.

phases.name: Across anxiety disorders
phases.caption: Pooled across studies, after CBT the caudate and part of the putamen were less active, and areas including the right dorsal anterior cingulate, the right orbitofrontal cortex and the right parahippocampal gyrus were more active during tasks.

order.rationale: This is a pooled analysis of before-and-after studies; it is shown first only to present the findings one at a time.

phases.name: Facing a social threat
phases.caption: In one study of social anxiety, the extra activity to angry faces in the right medial prefrontal cortex and right insula was reduced after CBT, as was activity in visual areas.

citations.authors: Klumpp H, Fitzgerald DA, Phan KL
citations.title: Neural predictors and mechanisms of cognitive behavioral therapy on threat processing in social anxiety disorder.
citations.quote: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was conducted during responses to social signals of threat (fearful/angry faces) against positive signals (happy faces) in 14 patients with SAD before and after 12 weeks of CBT.

phases.name: Rethinking a negative thought
phases.caption: In another study, while deliberately rethinking a negative belief about themselves, the left dorsolateral and the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex increased from before to after CBT, but not in people still waiting for therapy, and people felt less negative.

order.rationale: This is a separate study with a different task. It is placed after the other findings only to show them one at a time.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: The direction of change depends on the task: the medial prefrontal cortex went down while facing threat but up while rethinking. Some of the people in these studies did not improve.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: The right dorsomedial prefrontal cortex was more active than in people without social anxiety while viewing angry faces before treatment, and less active after CBT, in one study of 14 people. In a randomised trial (about 60 people scanned), the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex it was more active after CBT while reacting to and rethinking negative beliefs about themselves. The direction depends on the task.
